title: Container Runtime Security
summary: Container runtime security covers what happens after an image has started: the system calls a container makes, the privileges it holds, the files it tries to write, and the network connections it opens. The runtime is the component that actually creates the container process, so it is the last place where behaviour can be observed and blocked before the kernel acts. In production it appears as seccomp profiles, Linux capabilities dropped to a minimum, read only root filesystems, and an agent that turns suspicious process behaviour into an alert or a kill. The typical mistake is to assume that a scanned image and a namespace boundary are enough, because a container running as root with the default capability set and no seccomp profile still offers a wide kernel interface to anything that achieves code execution inside it.

beginner.definition: Container runtime security focuses on a container while it is running, not before it starts. It watches what the program inside tries to do, such as opening files or starting new processes. It also limits what the container is allowed to do. The runtime is the part of the platform that starts the container.
beginner.whyItMatters: A clean image can still be attacked after it starts. A program with a bug may let an intruder run commands inside the container. If the container has too much power, that intruder can reach the host. Runtime controls limit the damage and give you warning. They are the last line before the operating system itself is affected.
howItWorks: The platform starts a container from an image and gives the process a limited set of powers.
A seccomp profile, short for secure computing mode, lists which system calls the container may make.
Linux capabilities are dropped, so the process cannot change the network or mount disks.
The root filesystem is mounted read only, so the program cannot rewrite its own files.
A monitoring agent watches processes, files, and connections inside the running container.
Rules turn unusual behaviour into an alert, and they can stop the container automatically.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel room with a key card. The guest may open the room door, use the lights, and watch television. The card does not open other rooms, the plant room, or the safe. If a guest finds a way to force the door, the card still limits where they can go. Runtime security is the hotel card system, plus the front desk that notices a card used in odd places.
takeaways: Scanning an image does not control what it does after it starts.
Fewer capabilities and a read only filesystem shrink the damage an intruder can cause.
Watching runtime behaviour gives you a chance to detect and stop an attack.

objectives: Explain what container runtime security covers and at which point it applies.
Describe what the container runtime does when a container starts.
Explain how seccomp profiles and dropped capabilities limit a container.
Identify the kinds of behaviour that runtime monitoring looks for.
Recognise why a scanned image alone does not make a workload safe.
